Estimating and interpreting variance components in GAMs

Source: vignettes/articles/variance-components.Rmd
variance-components.Rmd

Use variance_comp() to answer two questions. How strongly does the model penalise its smooth and random-effect coefficients? How much do the fitted contributions of its terms vary across the observations? The first is about the model’s coefficients. The second also depends on the observed covariate values. A linear term, for example, varies more across observations that cover a wider range of its covariate, even with the same coefficient.

Load {gratia} and {mgcv}, then simulate 360 observations in 12 groups of 30. We generate z from x plus noise so the two are positively correlated. We generate w independently for the nonlinear effect.

library("gratia")
load_mgcv()

set.seed(2026)
dat <- data.frame(x = runif(360, -1, 1), w = runif(360),
  group = factor(rep(seq_len(12), each = 30)))
dat$z <- 0.8 * dat$x + rnorm(360, sd = 0.2)

The response combines positive linear effects of x and z with a sine wave in w. Add a Gaussian random intercept with standard deviation 0.6, shared by all observations in the same group, and independent Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.4 for each observation. The two linear effects tend to increase together, so their covariance increases the variance of their sum.

group_effect <- rnorm(12, sd = 0.6)
dat$y <- 2 * dat$x + 1.5 * dat$z + sin(2 * pi * dat$w) +
  group_effect[dat$group] + rnorm(360, sd = 0.4)

Fit a model with unpenalised linear terms for x and z, a smooth for w and a random intercept for group.

model <- gam(y ~ x + z + s(w, k = 8) + s(group, bs = "re"),
  data = dat, method = "REML")

Extract penalty variances and variances of fitted terms

First extract the penalty variances, which describe shrinkage of the penalised coefficients. The .lower_ci and .upper_ci columns give interval limits on the standard deviation scale.

vc_penalty <- variance_comp(model, type = "penalty")
vc_penalty
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   .component .variance .std_dev .lower_ci .upper_ci
#>   <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 s(w)         139.      11.8       6.51     21.3  
#> 2 s(group)       0.293    0.542     0.354     0.829
#> 3 scale          0.157    0.397     0.368     0.428

A penalty variance is the model scale \phi divided by the smoothing parameter \lambda_j. By default, the function expresses \lambda_j on the scale of the original penalty matrix, undoing the rescaling mgcv applies during fitting. For a given penalty, a larger variance corresponds to less shrinkage. There is one row per penalty, so a smooth can have several rows. For this Gaussian model the scale row gives the estimated residual variance. The unpenalised terms x and z appear in the fitted term table below.

With type = "terms", we measure how much each term’s fitted contribution varies across the observations used to fit the model. We use 1,000 draws of the coefficients to calculate intervals and set a seed to make the draws reproducible.

vc_terms <- variance_comp(model, type = "terms", n_draws = 1000, seed = 42)
vc_terms
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   .component .variance .std_dev .lower_ci .upper_ci .proportion
#>   <chr>          <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 x              1.33     1.15      1.05      1.25       0.527 
#> 2 z              0.497    0.705     0.602     0.810      0.312 
#> 3 s(w)           0.497    0.705     0.665     0.747      0.115 
#> 4 s(group)       0.265    0.515     0.477     0.557      0.0466
#> 5 total          3.83     1.96      1.91      2.00       1     
#> # ℹ 2 more variables: .proportion_lower_ci <dbl>, .proportion_upper_ci <dbl>

These are sample variances on the linear predictor scale, with each observation counted equally. The output includes unpenalised terms and has one row for each smooth, even if it has several penalties. Intercepts, offsets and residual variation are excluded from the calculation.

Account for covariance when comparing terms

The variance of the sum depends on both the term variances and their covariances. Let f_j be term j’s fitted values, F = \sum_j f_j their sum, and C their covariance matrix. Then

\operatorname{Var}(F) = \sum_j C_{jj} + 2\sum_{j<k} C_{jk}.

The result stores the covariance matrix of the fitted contributions across observations. Summing its diagonal gives the sum of the term variances. Summing all entries also accounts for covariance, so it gives the total variance of the combined contributions.

C <- attr(vc_terms, "covariance")
c(sum_of_term_variances = sum(diag(C)),
  total_including_covariance = sum(C))
#>      sum_of_term_variances total_including_covariance 
#>                   2.588591                   3.829474

To divide the total among terms, we split each covariance contribution, 2C_{jk}, equally between the two terms. Each term receives its own variance plus its covariance with every other term, expressed as the proportion p_j = \operatorname{Cov}(f_j, F) / \operatorname{Var}(F). When the total variance is positive, the proportions sum to one. Check this by computing only the individual proportions with include_total = FALSE and skipping interval calculation with n_draws = 0.

vc_no_total <- variance_comp(model, type = "terms", include_total = FALSE,
  n_draws = 0)
sum(vc_no_total$.proportion)
#> [1] 1

Intervals for the penalty variances account for uncertainty in the estimated smoothing parameters and model scale. For intervals on the fitted term variances, we draw all coefficients together from their approximate Gaussian posterior distribution. We recompute the fitted contributions and their variances and proportions for each draw. The smoothing parameters stay fixed at their estimates by default. Use unconditional = TRUE to include a correction for uncertainty in smoothing parameter estimates when the fitted model supports it. The proportions from each draw are in attr(vc_terms, "proportion_draws")$total. The interval limits describe each term separately, so the limits need not sum to one.

Plot term variances and their proportions

Use {patchwork} to show the variances, including the total, alongside the proportions for the individual terms. Both plots show intervals, with terms on the x-axis.

patchwork::wrap_plots(
  draw(vc_terms),
  draw(vc_terms, type = "proportion", include_total = FALSE),
  ncol = 2
)

Use draw(vc_penalty) for penalty variances or draw(vc_terms, type = "std_dev") for term standard deviations. draw() uses the stored intervals, squaring standard deviation limits when plotting variances. Use n_dodge = 2 to stagger term labels, angle = 45 to rotate them, or flip = TRUE to put terms on the y-axis.

Why a term’s proportion can be negative

To show how a proportion can be negative, we reuse the correlated x and z but give their effects opposite signs. The new response combines 2 * x - z with Gaussian noise of standard deviation 0.1, so the two effects partly cancel each other.

set.seed(208)
dat$contrast <- 2 * dat$x - dat$z + rnorm(nrow(dat), sd = 0.1)

Fit both linear terms and plot their proportions with intervals, omitting the total row.

opposing <- gam(contrast ~ x + z, data = dat, method = "REML")
vc_opposing <- variance_comp(opposing, type = "terms", n_draws = 1000, seed = 43)
draw(vc_opposing, type = "proportion", include_total = FALSE)

Their negative covariance reduces the variance of their sum. Accounting for this covariance gives x a share of 1.5 and z a share of -0.5. In this example z gets a negative proportion because its covariance with the contribution of x is more negative than its own variance is positive. The proportions still sum to one, so x gets a proportion greater than one. When the total variance is zero, the proportions are undefined (NA).
